item.title: Bioscoop demo: split screen to visualize color grading
item.description:
youtube

In this video, I demonstrate how I use Bioscoop, a Domain-Specific Language (DSL) for FFmpeg, to visualize color grading on @TheHaikouDiaries. The workflow is Emacs-based, where a Clojure REPL lives [00:11]. To effectively compare original footage with color-graded clips, I showcase two specific Clojure functions: side-by-side [00:48]: This function splits the video output into two streams (A and B). Stream A receives the color grading filter graph, while Stream B remains untouched. Both are scaled to 50% of their original size and stacked horizontally to display side-by-side. single-screen [01:28]: Similar to the first function, but instead of scaling the images down, it crops half of each screen and combines them to form a single, split view. I then provides a practical demonstration using a black-and-white filter graph to show how both the side-by-side [02:05] and single-screen [02:47] outputs look when executed via ffplay. For viewers interested in learning more, I recommend visiting the Bioscoop GitHub repository [03:32] for full documentation and a paper detailing its implementation and philosophy. Links: https://github.com/danielsz/bioscoop @TheHaikouDiaries

item.description:

Some experiments with using LLMs in Emacs, and a demo of gptel's presets feature. We can do better than a linear, immutable, top-down chat interface to LLMs. gptel is an LLM client for Emacs. (https://gptel.org) A preset is a named collection of gptel settings and behaviors applied to an LLM query as a unit: they can change any aspect of LLM interaction on the fly, providing a flexible, customizable interface for most (text-based) things you'd need an LLM for. 00:13 LLMs as text transformations 01:19 LLM clients as shell commands 02:03 Software with too many options 03:00 Configuration files and (finally) a gptel preset 03:10 The tutor preset 04:31 Inside the Tutor preset 05:12 The Introspect preset 06:52 The JSON preset 07:35 Interlude I: How presets work 08:52 Redirection: source | gptel | destination 10:04 Source: the Expand preset 11:20 The Visible-Text preset 11:55 The Include preset 12:48 Interlude II: Adding dynamic behavior to presets 14:14 Destination: the Notify preset 14:51 The Rewrite preset 17:05 The Annotate preset 21:18 Presets as "agents" 24:37 Problems with the presets UI 26:02 Interlude III: Resources for presets 27:22 LLM UIs in Emacs: this ain't it Emacs packages showcased in this demo: - https://github.com/karthink/gptel - https://github.com/karthink/gptel-agent - https://github.com/karthink/gptel-annotate - https://github.com/karthink/gptel-preset-collection - https://github.com/kmontag/macher Emacs packages and settings used in this demo - Presentation software: https://github.com/positron-solutions/dslide - Visuals: https://github.com/minad/org-modern and https://github.com/rnkn/olivetti - Fancy Flymake UI: https://github.com/konrad1977/flyover - Font: Monaspace Neon - Emacs theme: ef-reverie ,#emacs #llm #llms #gptel

item.title: User Interface to Computer Applications Demonstrated in GNU Emacs
item.description:
youtube

This series of videos demonstrates an individual's ideas about the user interfaces to computer software. The claim is made that users could be served better with a more automated display system showing, in real time, both what is available, and what action is necessary to get things done. A personal system is shown as the demonstration vehicle; this system has been installed in the Emacs text editor for many years. The target consumers are programmers and system designers, who may find the ideas to be food for thought. The video was made in ten sessions, each with a theme. These sessions are available individually and also as a single aggregate video. Total run time is two hours and ten minutes. https://youtu.be/NqinYjlQ8Tk https://youtu.be/BJ060oT9ntQ https://youtu.be/ONkzXTzP9pE https://youtu.be/R08M-sVNR64 https://youtu.be/41DSFZHTwo4 https://youtu.be/vbOmRhNNvMc https://youtu.be/auFq-9am06o https://youtu.be/HDUlHNVINI0 https://youtu.be/hcgkL36u3UM https://youtu.be/x8Y9eQbkQms https://youtu.be/iaHdNhtvL3Y The video .mp4 files work very well when viewed in Xviewer running on GNU/Linux. However, there have been out-of-sync problems between video and audio when viewed in a web browser. The problems are irritations rather than anything more significant, but they may appear.
